title: India, Canada Open Fourth Round of Talks on Proposed Trade Pact
excerpt: The five-day round in New Delhi covering goods, services and rules of origin aims to conclude the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement by the end of 2026, with both sides targeting $50 billion in bilateral trade by 2030.
body:
• India and Canada began the fourth round of negotiations for a proposed Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) in New Delhi on September 14, running through September 18.
  • On the table: trade in goods, trade in services, rules of origin and technical barriers to trade — adding to earlier rounds on intellectual property, investment and regulatory cooperation.
  • Both sides aim to conclude the pact by the end of 2026, after July's third round in Ottawa.
  • Two-way merchandise trade dipped 8.22% to $7.95 billion in 2025–26, against a $50 billion bilateral trade target by 2030.

A five-day push in New Delhi

India and Canada opened the fourth round of talks for a proposed Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) in New Delhi on September 14, aiming to conclude the agreement this year, an official said, according to The Hindu.

The five-day round, running through September 18, takes up trade in goods and services, rules of origin and technical barriers to trade, following July's third round in Ottawa. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal and Canada's International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu have exchanged the negotiation framework in the presence of the two prime ministers.

"It was a delight to meet Prime Minister Carney on the sidelines of the Evian G7 Summit. In less than a year, it is our fourth meeting, indicating our commitment to strong India-Canada ties."

— Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India

Context and background

The relationship froze in 2023 after the killing of Khalistani separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada, with diplomats expelled and engagement suspended through much of 2024. The reset began this year.

Modi and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney have met four times in less than a year, most recently at the G7 summit in Evian, France, where they agreed to accelerate the CEPA talks and widen cooperation across trade, energy, defence, technology and talent mobility, per the Ministry of External Affairs.

Carney visited India in March, and in May Goyal led the largest-ever Indian business delegation to Canada. The leaders have also agreed to negotiate a General Security of Information Agreement, launched a "Raisina Americas" dialogue platform, and Modi backed Canada's IORA dialogue-partner bid. Modi has been invited to visit Canada later this year.

Impact and analysis

The economics need the pact. Two-way merchandise trade fell 8.22% to $7.95 billion in 2025–26 ($4.67 billion in Indian exports against $3.28 billion in imports), from $8.66 billion the year before, according to The Hindu. Hitting the official $50 billion-by-2030 target would require goods trade to more than sextuple — in May the two sides even spoke of doubling two-way trade to $70 billion by 2030, per Mint. Tariff cuts alone will not close the gap; services, investment and supply chains must do the heavy lifting.

India's exports to Canada rest on pharmaceuticals, iron and steel, seafood, cotton garments, electronics and chemicals; its main imports are pulses, pearls and semi-precious stones, coal, fertiliser, paper and petroleum crude. Services — telecom, computer and information services, and business services — are the fast-growing layer, where Indian IT and professional firms stand to gain most.

A tariff window has opened: Canada's retaliatory tariffs on US imports — 15%, 25% and 50% tranches from September 8 on steel, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics — could let Indian exporters pick up Canadian demand as buyers diversify away from US suppliers. India exported roughly $1 billion across those focus sectors to Canada in FY2026, per trade analysis carried by newkerala.

Energy frames the talks too: the leaders reviewed commercial arrangements around LNG, LPG and metallurgical coal and stressed resilient supply chains for global energy and food security — a signal that CEPA is being built as economic architecture, not just a tariff schedule.

Diaspora angle

Few trade deals land this directly in diaspora life. Canada hosts more than 425,000 Indian students and one of the largest Indian-origin communities outside India — and the services and mobility chapters feed into their job prospects, businesses and remittance costs.

The governments are pairing the talks with people-level moves: the Canada–India Talent and Innovation Strategy, a renewed consular dialogue, and future dialogues on defence, finance and migration. For the diaspora, that is the sign the thaw is institutional, not just diplomatic.

What's next

This round runs through September 18, with more expected before year-end. Rules of origin and technical barriers to trade — the chapters that decide how usable a pact actually is for businesses — are where talks typically slow, and they are squarely on this week's agenda.

On the calendar: a Canadian trade mission to India later this year led by Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, and a possible Modi visit to Canada. The year-end deadline is ambitious; whether it survives the technical chapters will define the next three months.
